newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine and EBRD continue Chernobyl closure talks.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine and EBRD continue Chernobyl closure talks.

text.p: Ukraine and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) completed two days of talks on Friday to discuss an agreement to close the Chernobyl nuclear power station and build two new reactors.

"The EBRD has been asked by President Kuchma to help finance the development of the energy sector in Ukraine," EBRD vice-president Ron Freeman told reporters after meetings with President Leonid Kuchma and Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko.
"The G7 have also asked the EBRD to take lead responsibility in this very, very important programme," he said, referring to the Group of Seven (G7) wealthy industrial nations.

The meetings ended just days after Ukrainian officials detected high neutron radiation readings inside the "sarcophagus", the structure covering the ruined fourth reactor at Chernobyl, site of the world's worst civil nuclear disaster.

Viktor Chebrov, head of Ukraine's nuclear authority, Derzhkomatom, played down concerns on Friday over the neutron activity but repeated calls to build a new sarcophagus, Interfax Ukraine news agency reported.

Ukraine and the EBRD are working on a deal to finance Chernobyl's closure, replace electricity output lost by the closure by building two new reactors at the Khmelnitsky and Rivne plants, and repair the concrete "sarcophagus" encasing reactor Number Four.
Freeman said the EBRD has asked "internationally known experts" to provide recommendations by November 29.
"We will follow up from their recommendations," he said.
The EBRD official did not say how much money was involved, although G7 nations have agreed to provide up to $3 billion for Ukraine to close the plant by the year 2000.
A spokesman for Lazarenko quoted the prime minister as saying Ukraine must bring the two new reactors, one in southwest Ukraine and the other in the west, into operation by the end of 1997.

"Ukraine plans to close 103 coal mines, and Chernobyl's first reactor will be taken out of operation by November. Ukraine must bring the two new reactors into operation by the end of 1997 so it does not lose its energy sector," he said.
Lazarenko told Freeman the Ukrainian government would guarantee credits to build the new reactors.

Chernobyl provides about five percent of Ukraine's electricity. The fourth reactor caught fire and exploded in 1986, spreading fallout over most of Europe, including large portions of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.

The EBRD also discussed helping Ukraine develop new business, increased aid to the agricultural sector to boost grain yields, and participation in oil and gas development on the Black Sea shelf, the spokesman said.
